lessons.title: Selecting Materials & Components
lessons.description: How designers choose the right material by balancing function, cost, ethics and aesthetics.
lessons.content_html:
Why Material Selection Matters

Every product begins with a choice: what material should it be made from? A designer must weigh up a range of factors before committing to timber, metal, polymer, textile or paper. The wrong choice can make a product too expensive, too fragile, or harmful to the environment. Exam questions on material selection often ask you to justify why a specific material is suitable for a given product.

Key Fact

The six main factors in material selection are: functionality, aesthetics, availability, cost, environmental impact, and social & ethical considerations.

Functionality & Ease of Working

Functionality is the starting point. A material must be fit for purpose. A kitchen chopping board needs a food-safe, durable surface — hardwood such as beech works well because it resists scoring and does not taint food. A children's toy needs impact resistance and no sharp edges, making injection-moulded ABS polymer a common choice. Ease of working also matters: if a material is difficult to cut, shape or join, production costs rise.

Aesthetics: Finish, Texture & Colour

Aesthetics influence consumer appeal. Oak has a warm grain that suits furniture; brushed stainless steel gives kitchen products a modern feel; polyester fabric can be dyed in vibrant colours for sportswear. Designers match the look and feel of a material to the target market and product purpose.

Availability & Cost

Availability determines whether a material can be sourced reliably. Exotic hardwoods like ebony are beautiful but rare, which drives up cost and raises sustainability concerns. Mild steel, by contrast, is widely available and relatively cheap. Cost also depends on volume: bulk buying reduces the per-unit price, which matters for mass-produced items.

Timber: Softwoods (pine, spruce) are cheaper than hardwoods (oak, mahogany). MDF and plywood offer a low-cost manufactured alternative.

Metals: Mild steel is inexpensive; aluminium costs more but is lighter. Copper and brass are costlier still.

Polymers: Polypropylene and HDPE are among the cheapest. Acrylic and nylon cost more but offer better mechanical properties.

Textiles: Cotton and polyester are affordable. Silk, wool and Kevlar are premium-priced.

Papers & boards: Cartridge paper and corrugated card are low-cost. Foil-lined board for food packaging costs more due to added barrier layers.

Environmental Factors

Designers must consider a material's environmental impact throughout its life. Can it be recycled at end of life? Is it made from renewable sources? Timber from FSC-certified forests is a responsible choice. Recycled aluminium uses only 5% of the energy needed to produce virgin aluminium, making it a strong environmental option for drinks cans and packaging.

Key Fact

Selecting materials with end-of-life disposal in mind is a key exam theme. Products that can be recycled, composted or disassembled for reuse score highly in sustainability assessments.

Social, Cultural & Ethical Factors

Social responsibility means ensuring a material does not cause harm during extraction, processing or disposal. Products should be safe for workers to manufacture and safe for consumers to use. Cultural sensitivity matters too — certain materials or animal-derived products may be inappropriate for some markets. Ethical sourcing, such as buying FSC timber or Fairtrade cotton, shows a designer is thinking beyond profit.

A furniture company choosing timber should look for the FSC logo, which guarantees the wood comes from responsibly managed forests. A clothing brand might use Fairtrade cotton to ensure farmers receive a fair wage. In metals, conflict minerals (such as cobalt mined in unsafe conditions) are a growing concern — responsible manufacturers audit their supply chains.

Putting It All Together

In practice, material selection is always a trade-off. A lightweight polymer might be cheap and easy to mould, but it is not biodegradable. A natural hardwood is attractive and renewable, but expensive and harder to work. The best designers balance all six factors — functionality, aesthetics, availability, cost, environment and ethics — to find the optimum material for each product.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to justify a material choice, structure your answer around at least three selection factors (e.g. functionality, cost, environment). Name the specific material, state the property that makes it suitable, and link that property to the product’s requirements. Avoid vague statements like “it is strong” — say why strength matters for that product.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Six selection factors: functionality, aesthetics, availability, cost, environmental impact, and social/ethical considerations must all be weighed when choosing a material.
  • Trade-offs are inevitable: no single material scores top marks on every factor — designers must prioritise based on the product’s purpose and target market.
  • End-of-life matters: choosing recyclable, reusable or biodegradable materials reduces a product’s environmental footprint.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'functionality' in the context of material selection.
practice_questions.marks: The suitability of a material for its intended purpose/application (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two aesthetic factors a designer might consider when selecting a material for a piece of furniture.
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each valid aesthetic factor described, e.g.: Surface grain/texture of the wood gives a natural, warm appearance (1). Colour of the material matches the design style or interior decor (1). Surface finish such as gloss or matt affects visual appeal (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer might choose FSC-certified timber over non-certified timber when manufacturing a bookcase.
practice_questions.marks: FSC certification ensures timber comes from sustainably managed forests (1) where trees are replanted to maintain the ecosystem (1). This appeals to environmentally conscious consumers and can improve brand reputation (1). Using certified timber also helps reduce deforestation and supports ethical forestry practices (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why cost is not always the most important factor when selecting a material for a product. Use examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Detailed explanation with relevant examples. E.g. A children’s toy must prioritise safety over cost — ABS polymer is more expensive than some alternatives but it is non-toxic, impact resistant and has no sharp edges when moulded (up to 3). Environmental regulations may require recyclable materials even if they cost more (1). Ethical sourcing (Fairtrade cotton, FSC timber) adds cost but meets consumer expectations and legal requirements (1). A cheap material that fails in use damages brand reputation and costs more in returns/replacements (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic points with limited or no examples.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of recycled polymers versus virgin polymers for manufacturing food packaging. Consider functionality, cost and environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation covering all three factors with a supported conclusion. Recycled polymers reduce landfill waste and use less energy in production, lowering environmental impact. However, recycled polymers may have inconsistent properties and some are not food-safe without additional processing. Virgin polymers offer reliable, consistent quality and meet food safety regulations but contribute to fossil fuel depletion. Cost of recycled can be lower (reduced raw material) or higher (processing to food-grade). Conclusion weighing both sides.
Mid band (4-6): Covers at least two factors with some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): Limited points, mainly descriptive.

practice_questions.text: A company is designing a new range of outdoor garden chairs. Discuss the factors that would influence the selection of materials for this product. In your answer, consider at least four different selection factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion of 4+ factors with specific material examples and a clear conclusion. Factors include: functionality (weather resistance, UV stability, strength — e.g. treated softwood, HDPE, powder-coated aluminium), aesthetics (colour range, texture, modern vs traditional look), cost (budget vs premium range, bulk production savings), environmental impact (recyclable materials, FSC timber, recycled polymers), availability (standard stock forms, supplier reliability), ethical/social (safe manufacturing, fair labour). spelling/grammar: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar throughout.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good discussion of 3–4 factors with examples.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some relevant factors discussed, limited examples.
Lower band (1-3): Basic or superficial points. spelling/grammar errors.

lessons.title: Forces & Stresses
lessons.description: Tension, compression, bending, torsion and shear — and how materials resist them.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Forces & Stresses?

Every product experiences forces during use. A shelf bears weight, a bridge resists wind, a chair withstands the sitter's mass. Understanding the five main types of force helps designers choose materials and shapes that will not fail. You need to identify, explain and apply these forces to real products across all material categories.

Key Fact

The five types of force and stress are: tension (pulling apart), compression (pushing together), bending (a combination of tension and compression), torsion (twisting), and shear (sliding forces in opposite directions).

The Five Forces Explained

Tension occurs when a material is pulled from both ends. Think of a washing line holding wet clothes, or the steel cables on a suspension bridge. Materials under tension are being stretched.

Compression is the opposite — a squashing force. The legs of a table experience compression from the weight of items placed on top. Concrete is strong in compression, which is why it is used for building foundations.

Bending combines tension and compression. When you stand on a plank supported at both ends, the top surface is compressed and the bottom surface is in tension. If the material cannot resist both, it snaps.

Torsion is a twisting force. A screwdriver shaft experiences torsion when you turn it. The key to resisting torsion is using a solid cross-section or a tube — hollow circular sections are especially efficient.

Shear acts when two forces push in opposite directions along parallel planes. Scissors work by applying shear force to paper. A rivet holding two metal sheets together resists shear as the sheets try to slide apart.

Forces Across Material Categories

Timber: Good in compression along the grain but weaker across it. Plywood resists forces in multiple directions because its layers are glued with alternating grain.

Metals: Steel has excellent tensile strength, making it ideal for cables and structural beams. Cast iron is strong in compression but brittle under tension.

Polymers: Thermoplastics like polypropylene flex rather than snap, absorbing bending forces. Rigid polymers like acrylic can shatter under impact.

Textiles: Woven fabrics resist tension along the warp and weft. Knitted fabrics stretch more, making them better for products that flex.

Papers & boards: Corrugated card resists compression because the fluted inner layer acts as a series of small arches.

Reinforcing & Stiffening Materials

Materials can be modified to better resist forces. You need to know specific techniques and explain why they work.

Key Fact

Common reinforcement methods include: lamination (gluing layers together), folding (creating flanges or channels), webbing (adding ribs or gussets), and fabric interfacing (bonding stiffening material to textiles).

Lamination: Gluing thin layers of material together increases strength. Plywood is a classic example — odd numbers of veneers with alternating grain direction resist warping and cracking. Laminated steel is used in transformer cores.

Bending and folding: A flat sheet of metal is weak in bending, but fold it into an L-shape or a box section and it becomes far stiffer. Corrugated card uses the same principle — the wave-shaped flute resists compression.

Webbing and gussets: Triangular gusset plates at the corners of a shelf bracket spread the load and prevent the joint from collapsing. Internal ribs in plastic mouldings add stiffness without much extra weight.

Fabric interfacing: Iron-on interfacing is bonded to textile panels (e.g. collar and cuffs) to add structure and resist deformation.

Changing Magnitude & Direction of Forces

Designers can redirect or reduce forces using structural shapes. An arch converts a downward load into compression along its curve, pushing outward into its supports. A triangulated frame (like a roof truss) distributes loads efficiently because triangles cannot be deformed without changing the length of a side. I-beams concentrate material at the top and bottom flanges where bending stress is greatest, saving weight in the middle.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering a question about forces, always name the specific force (tension, compression, bending, torsion or shear), explain how it acts on the product, and describe how the material or structure resists it. A common mistake is writing “the material is strong” without saying which type of force it resists or why its shape helps.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Five forces: tension (pull), compression (push), bending (flex), torsion (twist) and shear (slide) — learn to identify each in real products.
  • Material matters: different materials resist different forces better — steel excels in tension, concrete in compression, plywood resists forces in multiple directions.
  • Reinforcement techniques: lamination, folding, webbing/gussets and interfacing all improve a material’s ability to handle forces.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'shear force'.
practice_questions.marks: Two forces acting in opposite directions close together, causing a material to slide or tear apart (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between tension and compression.
practice_questions.marks: Tension is a pulling force that stretches a material (1). Compression is a pushing force that squashes or shortens a material (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how corrugated card is able to resist compression forces.
practice_questions.marks: Corrugated card has a wave-shaped (fluted) inner layer (1) sandwiched between two flat liner layers (1). The flutes act like a series of small arches (1) which distribute the compressive load and prevent the card from crushing flat (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why plywood is stronger than a single piece of timber of the same thickness. Refer to its structure in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Detailed explanation. Plywood is made from thin layers (veneers) glued together (1) with the grain direction alternating at 90° in each layer (1). Natural timber is strongest along the grain and weak across it (1). By alternating the grain, plywood resists forces in multiple directions (1), reducing the risk of splitting or warping (1). An odd number of layers ensures the board is balanced and stable (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic understanding of layers/grain.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of lamination as a method of reinforcing materials. Refer to at least two material categories in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation with examples from 2+ categories and a conclusion. Timber: plywood resists warping and multi-directional forces, but adds thickness and weight. Metals: laminated steel reduces eddy currents in transformer cores, but delamination can occur over time. Textiles: laminated fabrics (e.g. Gore-Tex) combine waterproofing with breathability, but can be expensive and hard to recycle. Polymers: laminated layers in packaging provide barrier properties. Conclusion on when lamination is most/least effective.
Mid band (4-6): Examples from at least one category with some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): Limited description, few or no examples.

practice_questions.text: A designer is creating a lightweight shelving unit for a child’s bedroom. Discuss the forces the shelf will experience and how the designer could reinforce the structure to prevent failure.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion identifying specific forces (bending from weight on shelf, compression in uprights, shear at joints) with reinforcement solutions (gusset plates at corners, box-section uprights, laminated/manufactured board for shelves). Considers material choice (lightweight yet strong — e.g. plywood, aluminium). Links reinforcement to specific forces. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good identification of forces and some reinforcement methods.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Basic identification of forces with limited solutions.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial points, spelling/grammar errors.

lessons.title: Ecological & Social Footprint
lessons.description: The environmental and social impact of designing, manufacturing and disposing of products.
lessons.content_html:
What Is an Ecological Footprint?

Every product leaves a mark on the planet. From the moment raw materials are extracted to the point a product is thrown away, resources are consumed and pollution is created. An ecological footprint measures this impact. In AQA Design & Technology, you must understand the ecological and social issues that designers face — and how they can reduce harm.

Key Fact

Key ecological issues include: deforestation (timber), mining (metals and minerals), drilling (crude oil for polymers), and farming (cotton and other natural fibres). Each process damages habitats, consumes energy and produces waste.

Product Miles & Carbon Footprint

The distance a product travels during its life — from raw material source, through manufacture and distribution, to the consumer and finally to disposal — is sometimes called product miles. Every stage of transportation burns fuel and releases carbon dioxide. A cotton T-shirt might involve cotton grown in India, spun into yarn in Bangladesh, dyed in China, assembled in Vietnam, and sold in the UK — racking up thousands of miles before a customer puts it on.

Carbon is also produced during manufacture itself. Smelting aluminium, firing ceramics, and injection moulding polymers all require significant energy. Designers can reduce carbon output by choosing local suppliers, using renewable energy in manufacture, and selecting materials with lower carbon footprint.

The Six Rs

The six Rs provide a framework for sustainable design. They appear frequently in the AQA exam and you should be able to explain each one with examples.

Key Fact

The six Rs are: Reduce, Refuse, Re-use, Repair, Recycle, and Rethink.

Reduce: Use fewer materials or less energy. Lightweighting packaging (thinner plastic bottles, smaller boxes) reduces waste and transport costs.

Refuse: Reject materials or processes that cause unnecessary harm. A manufacturer might refuse to use single-use plastic and switch to compostable alternatives.

Re-use: Design products for multiple uses. Glass milk bottles, refillable water bottles and modular furniture can all be used again rather than discarded.

Repair: Design products so they can be fixed rather than replaced. Fairphone makes smartphones with replaceable modules so users can swap a broken screen instead of buying a new phone.

Recycle: Use materials that can be reprocessed into new products. Aluminium cans, PET bottles and cardboard are widely recycled. Designers should mark products with recycling codes and use mono-materials where possible to simplify recycling.

Rethink: Question whether the product is needed at all, or whether a radically different approach would work. Digital tickets replace printed card tickets; e-books replace printed textbooks.

Social Issues in Design & Manufacture

A product’s social footprint covers how it affects people. Designers must consider safe working conditions in factories, fair wages for workers, and the impact of pollution on local communities. The 2013 Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh killed over 1,100 garment workers and exposed dangerous conditions in the global textile supply chain.

Safe working conditions: Manufacturers should comply with health and safety regulations, provide protective equipment, and avoid excessive working hours.

Reducing pollution: Factories should treat wastewater before discharge, control air emissions, and manage chemical waste responsibly. Textile dyeing, for example, can pollute rivers if effluent is untreated.

Ethical sourcing: Using Fairtrade materials, FSC-certified timber, or conflict-free minerals ensures that raw material supply chains do not exploit workers or communities.

Designing for inclusivity: Products should be accessible to users of different ages, abilities and cultural backgrounds. Reducing negative social impact also means avoiding designs that promote harmful stereotypes.

Choosing Appropriate Energy Sources

Switching from fossil fuels to renewable energy (solar, wind, hydroelectric) during manufacture reduces a product’s ecological footprint. Some companies offset their carbon emissions by investing in tree planting or renewable energy projects. However, the most effective strategy is to reduce energy use in the first place — through efficient machinery, shorter supply chains, and lightweight product design.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on sustainability often ask you to explain or evaluate how a designer can reduce a product’s ecological footprint. Always reference the six Rs by name and give specific product examples. A common mistake is listing the six Rs without explaining how each one applies to the product in the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ecological footprint covers deforestation, mining, drilling and farming — plus the carbon produced during manufacture, transport and disposal.
  • The six Rs (Reduce, Refuse, Re-use, Repair, Recycle, Rethink) are a framework for sustainable design that you must know with examples.
  • Social footprint means considering worker safety, fair wages, pollution and ethical sourcing throughout the supply chain.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ecological footprint'.
practice_questions.marks: The total environmental impact of a product throughout its entire life, from raw material extraction to disposal (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways a designer could reduce the product miles of a new table lamp.
practice_questions.marks: Source materials from local/UK suppliers to reduce transport distance (1). Manufacture the product in the same country where it will be sold (1). Also accept: use lightweight materials to reduce fuel consumption during transport.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the 'Repair' principle from the six Rs can reduce a product's environmental impact. Use an example.
practice_questions.marks: If a product can be repaired, it lasts longer (1) so fewer replacement products need to be manufactured, saving raw materials and energy (1). For example, Fairphone designs smartphones with replaceable modules (1) so a broken screen can be swapped without discarding the whole phone, reducing electronic waste (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the social issues a clothing manufacturer should consider when producing garments overseas.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Detailed explanation covering multiple issues. Safe working conditions — factories must meet health and safety standards, provide fire exits, and limit working hours (up to 2). Fair wages — workers should receive at least the minimum wage for their country and not be exploited (1). Pollution — textile dyeing can release harmful chemicals into rivers, affecting local communities (1). Child labour — some supply chains use underage workers, which is illegal and unethical (1). The Rana Plaza collapse (2013) shows the consequences of poor conditions (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic points with limited detail.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of recycling as a strategy for reducing a product's ecological footprint.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Benefits: diverts waste from landfill, conserves raw materials, recycled aluminium uses 95% less energy than virgin. Limitations: not all materials are easily recyclable (composites, mixed polymers), contamination reduces quality, recycling still requires energy and transport, downcycling means material quality degrades. Some materials (thermosetting polymers) cannot be recycled at all. Conclusion on effectiveness vs other strategies (reduce, re-use).
Mid band (4-6): Some benefits and limitations discussed.
Lower band (1-3): Basic description, one-sided argument.

practice_questions.text: A company wants to redesign its product packaging to be more sustainable. Discuss how the six Rs could be applied to reduce the packaging’s ecological and social footprint.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive application of all six Rs with specific packaging examples. Reduce: use thinner/lighter materials, smaller box sizes. Refuse: eliminate unnecessary layers like plastic windows. Re-use: design boxes customers can repurpose. Repair: not always applicable to packaging but reusable containers can be maintained. Recycle: switch to mono-materials (all cardboard) with clear recycling symbols. Rethink: could digital instructions replace printed inserts? Social: ensure cardboard from FSC sources, factory workers have safe conditions. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good application of 4–5 Rs with examples.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some Rs applied, limited examples.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial, spelling/grammar errors.

lessons.title: Sources, Origins & Life Cycle Assessment
lessons.description: Where materials come from, how they are processed, and how LCA measures environmental impact.
lessons.content_html:
Where Do Materials Come From?

Every material in a product starts as a raw resource extracted from the earth, grown in a field, or harvested from an animal. You need to know the primary source of each material category and the main processes involved in converting it into a workable form.

Sources & Origins by Category

Paper is made from cellulose fibres derived from wood (mainly softwood trees like spruce and pine) and sometimes grasses such as bamboo. Logs are chipped, pulped in water with chemicals, and the resulting slurry is pressed, dried and rolled into sheets. Recycled paper skips the tree-felling stage by re-pulping waste paper, though each cycle shortens the fibres and reduces quality.

Trees are felled and converted into usable planks through conversion (sawing methods include through-and-through and quarter sawn). The green timber must then be seasoned — either air-dried (stacked outdoors for months) or kiln-dried (heated in a controlled chamber for days). Manufactured boards like MDF, plywood and chipboard are made from timber waste — fibres, veneers or chips bonded with resin.

Metals are extracted from ore mined from the earth. The ore is refined — iron ore is smelted in a blast furnace to produce pig iron, which is then converted into steel. Aluminium is extracted from bauxite ore using electrolysis, an extremely energy-intensive process. Copper ore is smelted and electrolytically refined to high purity. Alloys (e.g. brass = copper + zinc, stainless steel = iron + chromium + nickel) are created by mixing metals to improve properties.

Most polymers come from crude oil. Crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation. The naphtha fraction is then broken down further by cracking to produce monomers like ethene and propene. These monomers are then polymerised — joined into long chains — to create materials such as polyethylene, polypropylene and PVC.

Textile fibres come from three main sources. Animal sources: wool from sheep, silk from silkworms. Vegetable sources: cotton from the cotton plant, linen from flax. Chemical/synthetic sources: polyester and nylon from crude oil (same petrochemical route as polymers). Raw fibres are cleaned, carded (aligned), spun into yarn, and then woven or knitted into fabric.

Key Fact

You must know the primary source and the main conversion process for each material category: paper (cellulose from wood → pulping), timber (trees → conversion & seasoning), metals (ore → smelting/electrolysis), polymers (crude oil → fractional distillation & cracking), textiles (animal/vegetable/chemical → spinning).

Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)

A life cycle assessment (LCA) examines the environmental impact of a product at every stage: raw material extraction, processing, manufacture, distribution, use, and end-of-life disposal. It considers energy consumption, water use, carbon emissions, pollution and waste at each stage.

Key Fact

The five stages of an LCA are: 1. Raw material extraction → 2. Processing & manufacture → 3. Distribution & transport → 4. Use & maintenance → 5. End-of-life disposal (recycle, landfill or incinerate).

Why LCA Matters for Designers

An LCA helps designers make informed choices. If the biggest environmental impact of a kettle is the energy used to boil water (the "use" stage), then improving insulation to keep water hot longer would have a bigger effect than switching to a lighter plastic for the casing. LCA data can also reveal hidden problems — for example, a "biodegradable" polymer that only breaks down under industrial composting conditions, not in a home compost bin.
lessons.exam_tip_html: LCA questions often ask you to identify which stage has the greatest environmental impact for a specific product. Think carefully about the product’s life — for a car, manufacture and fuel use dominate; for a paper cup, raw material extraction and disposal are key. Always explain why a particular stage has the most impact.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Know the source of each material: paper from cellulose/wood, timber from trees (conversion + seasoning), metals from ore (smelting), polymers from crude oil (distillation + cracking), textiles from animal/vegetable/chemical sources (spinning).
  • LCA has five stages: extraction, processing, distribution, use, and end-of-life — each with its own environmental impact.
  • LCA guides design decisions: by revealing where the biggest environmental costs are, designers can focus improvements where they matter most.

practice_questions.text: Describe how crude oil is converted into a polymer such as polyethylene.
practice_questions.marks: Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation to produce naphtha (1). The naphtha is cracked to produce monomers (ethene) which are then polymerised into polyethylene (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why seasoning is an important process in the production of timber-based products.

practice_questions.text: Explain the benefits and limitations of using a life cycle assessment when designing a new product.

Upper band (4-6): Benefits: identifies which stage has the greatest environmental impact so the designer can focus improvements (1), helps compare materials objectively (1), supports marketing claims about sustainability (1). Limitations: LCA data can be complex and expensive to collect (1), results depend on assumptions (e.g. how long the product lasts) (1), does not always account for social factors (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the environmental impact of using metals versus polymers as packaging materials. Consider their sources, processing and end-of-life disposal.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced comparison. Metals: mining ore is destructive and energy-intensive, especially aluminium (electrolysis). However, metals are infinitely recyclable with significant energy savings (aluminium: 95% less energy). Polymers: derived from crude oil (non-renewable), cheaper and lighter (reduces transport emissions), but most are not easily recycled and persist in the environment for centuries. Some polymers (PET) are recyclable but contamination limits rates. Conclusion on which is more sustainable and under what conditions.
Mid band (4-6): Covers both materials with some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Basic, one-sided description.

practice_questions.text: A company manufactures single-use paper coffee cups. Carry out a simplified life cycle assessment of this product, identifying the environmental impact at each stage and suggesting improvements.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive LCA covering all five stages. Extraction: trees felled (deforestation, habitat loss) — use FSC timber. Processing: pulping uses water and chemicals, plastic liner added (hard to separate for recycling) — use water-based coatings. Distribution: lightweight but high-volume transport — flat-pack and local manufacture. Use: single use means short lifespan — consider reusable alternatives. End of life: plastic liner prevents standard paper recycling, most go to landfill — switch to compostable liner. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good coverage of 3–4 stages with improvements.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some stages covered, limited improvements.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial. spelling/grammar errors.

lessons.title: Stock Forms, Types & Sizes
lessons.description: Standard forms, sizes and components for timber, metals, polymers, textiles and papers.
lessons.content_html:
Why Stock Forms Matter

Materials are supplied in standard stock forms. Knowing what is available helps a designer calculate how much material to order, minimise waste, and ensure the product can be manufactured efficiently. You need to know the common stock forms, standard sizes and standard components for each material category.

Papers & Boards

Paper and board are sold in sheets and rolls. Standard sheet sizes follow the A-series (A0, A1, A2, A3, A4, A5). Board is measured by thickness (microns or mm), weight (gsm — grams per square metre), and colour. Corrugated card uses a ply rating (single, double, triple wall) to indicate strength. Standard components include fasteners (staples, paper clips), seals (adhesive strips) and bindings (spiral, saddle stitch).

Key Fact

Every material category has its own stock forms, standard sizes and standard components. You must be able to name examples from at least one category in the exam.

Timber-Based Materials

Timber is sold as planks, boards and standard mouldings (skirting, architrave, dowel). Sizes are specified by length, width, thickness and diameter (for dowel). Manufactured boards (MDF, plywood, chipboard) come in standard sheet sizes, typically 2440 × 1220 mm. Standard components include standard components such as woodscrews, hinges and KD (knock-down) fittings used in flat-pack furniture (e.g. cam locks, barrel nuts).

Metal-Based Materials

Metals are available as sheet, rod, bar and tube. They are sold by length, width, thickness and diameter. Standard components include rivets, machine screws, nuts and bolts. Metals are also available in standard profiles such as angle iron, channel and I-beam.

Polymers

Polymers come in many forms: sheet (acrylic, HIPS), rod, powder and granules (for injection moulding), foam (expanded polystyrene) and film (polythene bags). They are sold by length, width, gauge (thickness of film) and diameter. Standard components mirror those for metals — plastic screws, nuts, bolts and hinges are available for non-metal assemblies.

Textile-Based Materials

Textiles are sold as yarns (by weight and ply) and fabrics (by the roll or metre). Fabric is measured by roll size, width (typically 90 cm, 115 cm or 150 cm) and weight (gsm). Standard components include zips, press studs (poppers), Velcro, buttons and elastic.

Electronic and mechanical components are sold by quantity, voltage and current rating. Standard components include the E12 resistor series (12 preferred values per decade), dual in-line IC packages (DIL), and microcontrollers (PIC). These are ordered from specialist suppliers in standard packages.

Calculating Material Quantities

Designers must calculate how much material they need. This involves working out surface area (for sheet materials and coatings) and volume (for solid components). Efficient material use means considering nesting — arranging pattern pieces closely together on a sheet to minimise offcuts. This applies to timber sheets, metal plates, fabric layouts and card nets.

Key Fact

Nesting and efficient pattern spacing reduce material waste and save money, especially in batch and mass production where even small savings per unit add up across thousands of items.

A product requires six identical panels, each 300 mm × 200 mm. Standard MDF sheet size is 2440 mm × 1220 mm. Fitting 300 mm panels along the 2440 mm length gives 8 columns (8 × 300 = 2400 mm). Fitting 200 mm panels along the 1220 mm width gives 6 rows (6 × 200 = 1200 mm). That is 48 panels per sheet — so one standard sheet is more than enough for six panels, with material left over for other projects. Good nesting reduces waste to just 40 mm × 1220 mm + 2440 mm × 20 mm of offcuts.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Stock form questions may ask you to state the forms available for a material or to calculate how many components can be cut from a standard sheet. Always show your working in calculation questions — even if your final answer is wrong, you can still pick up method marks. Remember to account for waste and kerf (cutting width) where relevant.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stock forms vary by category: sheets, planks, rods, tubes, yarns, granules, films — know which forms apply to which material.
  • Standard components (screws, hinges, rivets, zips, KD fittings) are pre-made items used across all categories.
  • Efficient material use: calculate surface area or volume, use nesting to minimise waste, and buy standard sizes to reduce cost.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a furniture manufacturer would use KD (knock-down) fittings in a flat-pack bookcase.
practice_questions.marks: KD fittings allow the product to be assembled by the customer at home (1), so it can be shipped flat-packed, reducing packaging size and transport costs (1). The fittings are designed to be assembled and disassembled, so the bookcase can be moved or reconfigured (1). Standard KD components (cam locks, barrel nuts) are cheap, widely available and do not require specialist tools (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of nesting when cutting components from a standard sheet of material. Refer to both cost and waste in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Nesting means arranging pattern pieces as closely together as possible (1) to minimise the amount of unused material (offcuts) (1). This reduces waste, which is better for the environment (1). It also saves money because fewer sheets need to be purchased (1). In mass production, even a small saving per unit multiplied by thousands of products adds up to a significant cost reduction (1). The kerf (width of the cut) should also be accounted for in the nesting layout (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic understanding of nesting with limited detail.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of standard components versus custom-made components in product manufacturing.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Standard components: cheaper (mass-produced), readily available, consistent quality, easy to replace, simplify design. But: limited range of sizes/styles, may not fit a bespoke design, can make products look generic. Custom components: perfect fit for the design, unique aesthetics, can optimise performance. But: expensive to produce, longer lead times, harder to replace if broken. Conclusion on when each is most appropriate.
Mid band (4-6): Covers advantages and disadvantages of both with some evaluation.
Lower band (1-3): One-sided or superficial points.

practice_questions.text: A textile company is manufacturing 500 tote bags. Each bag requires a rectangle of fabric measuring 80 cm × 50 cm. The fabric is available in rolls 150 cm wide. Discuss how the company should plan the cutting layout to minimise waste, and calculate the minimum length of fabric needed.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Correct calculation with efficient layout. 150 cm width fits 1 bag (80 cm) plus another (80 cm would exceed 150 cm — OR could nest: 80+50=130 cm if rotated). Optimal: 3 pieces of 50 cm across the 150 cm width (3×50=150) with 80 cm length per row. That gives 3 bags per 80 cm. 500 ÷ 3 = 167 rows. 167 × 80 cm = 13,360 cm = 133.6 m minimum. Discussion of nesting strategy, seam allowances, fabric grain direction, pattern matching if printed, and kerf/cutting tolerance. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Reasonable calculation with some discussion of waste reduction.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Attempts calculation, limited discussion.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial or incorrect calculation. spelling/grammar errors.

lessons.title: Scales of Production
lessons.description: Prototype, batch, mass and continuous production — choosing the right scale for the job.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Scales of Production?

Not every product is made the same way. A one-off wedding cake and a million identical Mars bars require completely different manufacturing approaches. There are four scales of production: prototype, batch, mass and continuous. You must know what each one means, when it is used, and which processes suit each scale.

Key Fact

The four scales of production are: prototype (one-off), batch (set quantity), mass (large volume on an assembly line) and continuous (24/7 non-stop production).

Prototype (One-Off) Production

A prototype is a single item made to test a design. It is usually handmade using general-purpose tools and may take a long time to produce. The cost per unit is high because tooling and labour are not spread across many products. Examples include an architectural model, a bespoke piece of jewellery, or a 3D-printed concept model for a new phone case.

Batch Production

Batch production involves making a set number of identical items. Between batches, the equipment is reset or retooled for a different product. A bakery might produce 200 loaves of white bread, then switch to 150 wholemeal rolls. This is common in textiles (seasonal clothing runs), furniture (limited-edition ranges) and food manufacturing. Jigs and templates are used to maintain consistency within each batch.

Mass Production

Mass production uses assembly lines, automation and dedicated machinery to produce thousands or millions of identical items. The high initial investment in tooling (e.g. injection mould tools costing tens of thousands of pounds) is justified by the low unit cost when spread over huge volumes. Cars, smartphones, plastic bottles and printed circuit boards are all mass-produced. Quality control is built into the line — automated sensors check dimensions, weight and surface finish.

Timber: CNC routers and automated lathes produce identical wooden components at high speed. Flat-pack furniture uses standard panels cut and drilled by machine.

Metals: Stamping, pressing and die casting produce thousands of identical metal parts. Robotic welding assembles car bodies.

Polymers: Injection moulding is the most common mass-production process — molten polymer is forced into a mould, cooled and ejected. Cycle times can be as short as 30 seconds.

Textiles: Computer-controlled cutting tables and industrial sewing machines produce garments at volume. Automated looms weave fabric continuously.

Papers & boards: Offset lithography prints millions of identical sheets. Die-cutting machines stamp out packaging nets at high speed.

Continuous Production

Continuous production runs 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It is used when stopping and restarting the process would be extremely expensive or impractical. Examples include paper mills (continuous rolls of paper), steel production (blast furnaces run non-stop for years), oil refineries and electricity generation. The unit cost is the lowest of all scales, but flexibility is very limited — the line makes one product and changing it is costly.

Key Fact

The main difference between mass and continuous production is that mass production can be stopped and restarted (e.g. at the end of a shift), while continuous production runs non-stop because halting the process would damage equipment or waste materials.

Choosing the Right Scale

The choice of production scale depends on several factors: the number of products needed, the acceptable unit cost, the level of customisation required, and the available budget for tooling. A hand-thrown ceramic mug is beautiful but expensive; an injection-moulded plastic cup is cheap but lacks character. Designers must match the scale to the market.

Prototype: 1 item, highest unit cost, most flexible, general tools, skilled labour.

Batch: Tens to thousands, moderate unit cost, some flexibility (can switch products between batches), jigs and templates.

Mass: Thousands to millions, low unit cost, high tooling investment, assembly line, significant automation.

Continuous: Non-stop output, lowest unit cost, no flexibility, process cannot easily be stopped.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to recommend a scale of production, always name the scale, justify your choice by linking to the product volume and market, and name a suitable manufacturing process for that scale. For example: “Batch production using a jig on a pillar drill would be suitable because only 500 units are needed per month.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four scales: prototype (one-off), batch (set quantity), mass (assembly line) and continuous (24/7 non-stop) — each suits different product volumes and budgets.
  • Unit cost falls as volume rises because tooling and setup costs are spread across more products.
  • Scale determines process: hand tools for prototypes, jigs for batch, injection moulding for mass, and rolling mills for continuous.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'batch production'.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between mass production and continuous production.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the unit cost of a product decreases as the scale of production increases.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a small pottery studio producing handmade mugs would use a different scale of production to a company making disposable paper cups. Refer to specific scales in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:

The volume is low and customers pay a premium for the craftsmanship (1). The paper cup company uses continuous production (1) because demand is constant and high-volume, running 24/7 on automated machinery (1). Stopping the production line would waste materials and be expensive to restart (1).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate whether batch production or mass production would be more suitable for a company manufacturing school furniture. Consider cost, flexibility and product range.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Batch: allows different products (desks, chairs, shelving) to be made on the same equipment with retooling between runs; suits a range of sizes/styles; lower tooling investment. Mass: lower unit cost if demand is high enough; consistent quality; dedicated machinery. But: less flexible if the school wants custom sizes or finishes; high tooling cost only justified at very large volumes. Conclusion depends on order size and product variety.

Lower band (1-3): One-sided or superficial.

practice_questions.text: A small electronics company has designed a new phone case. Initially they expect to sell 200 units per month, but if successful, demand could rise to 50,000 units per month. Discuss how their manufacturing scale and processes should change as demand grows.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion. Initial phase: batch production at 200/month using 3D printing or CNC machining — low tooling cost, quick to start, easy to modify design. Growth phase: investment in injection mould tooling as demand reaches thousands/month — high upfront cost but low per-unit cost, fast cycle times. At 50,000/month, full mass production with dedicated moulds, automated quality control, robotic assembly. Discusses transition points, financial risk, and how design may need to change for different processes (e.g. draft angles for injection moulding). spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good discussion of at least two phases.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some relevant points but limited progression.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial. spelling/grammar errors.

lessons.title: Surface Treatments & Finishes
lessons.description: How finishes protect and enhance products across timber, metals, polymers and textiles.
lessons.content_html:
Why Apply a Surface Finish?

A raw material straight from the workshop is rarely ready for the consumer. Surface treatments and finishes serve two purposes: they protect the material from damage (corrosion, moisture, UV degradation, wear) and they enhance its appearance (colour, texture, gloss). You need to know specific finishes for each material category and be able to explain why each one is chosen.

Key Fact

Surface finishes have two key purposes: functional protection (preventing corrosion, rot, UV damage, moisture absorption) and aesthetic enhancement (improving colour, texture, gloss and visual appeal).

Papers & Boards

Printing is the primary finish for papers and boards — it adds colour, text and graphics. Embossing creates a raised pattern by pressing the material between shaped dies, giving a tactile quality used on greetings cards and luxury packaging. UV varnishing applies a glossy, scratch-resistant coating cured by ultraviolet light — often used on magazine covers and product boxes to make colours more vibrant and the surface more durable.

Timber-Based Materials

Painting covers the natural grain and provides a coloured, protective layer. Oil-based and water-based paints both seal the surface against moisture. Varnishing provides a transparent or tinted protective coat that shows the natural grain — polyurethane varnish is hard-wearing and water-resistant, making it ideal for tabletops and floors. Tanalising is a pressure treatment that forces preservative chemicals deep into the timber, protecting it against rot and insect attack. Tanalised timber is widely used for fencing, decking and garden furniture.

Metal-Based Materials

Metals are particularly vulnerable to corrosion (e.g. rust on steel, tarnishing on copper). Several finishes address this:

Dip coating: The metal component is heated and dipped into a tank of polymer powder or liquid plastic, which melts and forms a smooth, coloured coating. Used on tool handles, dish racks and playground equipment.

Powder coating: Dry polymer powder is sprayed onto the metal surface using an electrostatic charge, then baked in an oven to form a tough, even finish. It is more durable than paint and available in many colours. Used on bicycle frames, car wheels and metal furniture.

Galvanising: The metal is coated with a layer of zinc by hot-dip galvanising (dipping into molten zinc) or electro-galvanising. The zinc acts as a sacrificial layer — it corrodes before the steel underneath. Used on gates, crash barriers and roofing sheets.

Anodising: An electrochemical process that thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminium, making it harder and more resistant to corrosion. The porous surface can absorb dyes, allowing a range of colours. Used on aluminium window frames, phone cases and kitchen utensils.

Polymers

Polymers often need less finishing than metals or timber because they do not corrode or rot. However, finishes can still improve appearance and durability. Polishing (buffing with fine abrasive) creates a high-gloss finish on acrylic. Printing adds graphics to polymer surfaces — pad printing transfers ink from a silicone pad onto curved shapes (e.g. logos on bottle caps). Vinyl decals are adhesive graphics applied to polymer casings (phone cases, laptop covers, product branding).

Textile-Based Materials

Textiles are finished to add colour, pattern or functional properties. Printing applies colour designs to fabric using screen printing, digital printing or block printing. Dyeing saturates the entire fabric with colour — it can be done at the fibre, yarn or fabric stage. Stain protection (e.g. Scotchgard) applies a chemical coating that causes liquids to bead on the surface rather than soak in, protecting upholstery and outdoor clothing.

Key Fact

In the exam, you should be able to name at least one specific finish per material category and explain both its protective and aesthetic benefits.

Electronic & Mechanical Systems

PCB lacquering applies a protective conformal coating to printed circuit boards, shielding components from moisture, dust and chemical contamination. Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts in mechanical systems, preventing wear and overheating. Both are functional finishes with no aesthetic purpose.

The choice of finish depends on: the material category, the product's environment (indoor vs outdoor, wet vs dry), the desired appearance, cost, and whether the finish needs to be food-safe. Outdoor products need UV and weather resistance. Food-contact products need non-toxic, food-grade coatings. High-traffic surfaces need scratch and abrasion resistance.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Surface finish questions often ask you to explain or justify a finish for a specific product. Always state the finish by name (e.g. “powder coating”, not just “coating”), explain how it is applied, and describe both its protective and aesthetic benefits. A common mistake is describing the finish without linking it to the product’s requirements.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Two purposes: surface finishes protect materials (corrosion, moisture, UV, wear) and enhance appearance (colour, texture, gloss).
  • Know one finish per category: printing/UV varnishing (paper), painting/varnishing/tanalising (timber), dip/powder coating/galvanising (metal), polishing/vinyl decals (polymer), dyeing/stain protection (textile).
  • Match finish to product: consider the environment, durability needs, food safety and desired appearance when choosing a finish.

It can also add a gloss or satin sheen that makes the surface look polished and professional (1). Accept: painting adds colour; staining enhances grain with colour.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a manufacturer would choose powder coating rather than painting for a set of outdoor metal garden chairs.
practice_questions.marks: Powder coating produces a thicker, more even finish than paint (1). It is more resistant to chipping, scratching and fading from UV exposure (1), so it lasts longer in outdoor conditions (1). The electrostatic application ensures full coverage including hard-to-reach areas, and the baked finish is tough and weather-resistant (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why tanalising is used on timber for outdoor garden products. Describe the process and its benefits.
practice_questions.marks:
Upper band (4-6): Tanalising is a pressure treatment process (1). Timber is placed in a sealed chamber and chemical preservatives (e.g. copper-based compounds) are forced deep into the wood under pressure (1). This protects the timber against rot, fungal decay and insect attack (1). It extends the lifespan of outdoor products like fencing, decking and garden furniture significantly (1). The chemicals penetrate deep into the wood rather than just coating the surface, so even if the surface is scratched or cut, the interior is still protected (1). The greenish tint can fade over time, and the timber can still be painted or stained on top (1).
Lower band (1-3): Basic description of the process or benefits.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of dip coating versus galvanising as a surface treatment for a steel bike rack that will be installed outdoors.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-9): Balanced evaluation. Dip coating: provides a colourful, smooth polymer coating that resists corrosion and adds aesthetic appeal; soft coating absorbs minor impacts without chipping; but can be damaged by sharp scratches, exposing the steel beneath. Galvanising: zinc layer provides excellent long-term corrosion protection even if scratched (sacrificial protection); very durable; but limited colour options (silver/grey), rougher texture, less visually appealing. Both are suitable for outdoor use. Conclusion based on whether aesthetics or raw durability is the priority.
Mid band (4-6): Covers both finishes with some comparison.
Lower band (1-3): Describes one or both finishes with little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: A company is manufacturing a range of kitchen utensils (spatulas, spoons, tongs) from stainless steel with polymer handles. Discuss the surface treatments and finishes that should be applied to both the metal and polymer parts. Consider functional and aesthetic requirements.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (10-12): Comprehensive discussion. Metal parts: stainless steel already has corrosion resistance but may be polished to a mirror or brushed finish for aesthetics and hygiene (easy to clean). Food-safe requirement — no toxic coatings. Polymer handles: must be food-safe, heat-resistant, comfortable grip. Soft-touch overmoulding or textured finish for grip; colour through the polymer (pigmented granules) rather than surface paint which could chip into food. Dip coating could add colour but must be food-grade. Discusses: food safety regulations, dishwasher resistance, heat tolerance near cooking surfaces, brand identity through colour. spelling/grammar accurate.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good discussion covering both materials.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Covers one material well, other briefly.
Lower band (1-3): Superficial. spelling/grammar errors.

glossary_terms.definition: Applying ink designs to paper or card surfaces using methods such as offset lithography, screen printing or digital printing.
Creating a raised or recessed pattern on paper or card by pressing it between shaped dies.
Applying a glossy, protective ultraviolet-cured coating to paper or card to improve durability and appearance.
Pressure-treating timber with chemical preservatives to protect it against rot, fungal decay and insect attack.
The gradual degradation of a metal caused by chemical reactions with its environment, such as rusting of steel.
Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc to protect it from corrosion.
A chemical treatment applied to textile fibres or fabrics to repel liquids and resist staining.
